rationale: Although this qualitative expert-interview case study of Lusaka Water Supply and Sanitation Company (LWSC) addresses urban household water supply access, availability, and continuity (C1=yes, C3=yes, C4=yes), it fails Criterion 2 under the active narrow rule-type reading (C2_narrow=no, E03). The abstract explicitly defines both the analytical focus and findings around environmental, demographic, and physical source-water stressors—climate change (droughts and erratic rainfall), rapid population growth straining infrastructure capacity, and unplanned land development causing groundwater pollution in shallow water tables—rather than legal, regulatory, tariff, tenure/documentation, enforcement, or administrative rules governing household water access.
plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading, the study is excluded (E03) because its examined explanatory factors are climatic, demographic, and hydrogeological pressures on bulk supply and raw groundwater quality (erratic rainfall/droughts, rapid population growth, and aquifer pollution from unplanned development), with land-use planning regulation mentioned only as a generic concluding policy recommendation rather than an analysed legal/administrative service-access mechanism. Under the literal/plain Criterion 2 wording, a qualitative case study of LWSC addressing unplanned land development, sustainable utility management, and land-use planning regulations could plausibly discuss broader institutional or planning governance factors on full text, yielding 'unsure'.

evidence_quotes.quote: Despite a population of 3,079,964, only 134,807 household connections were established by LWSC in 2022.
The findings of the study reveal that climate change, population growth, and land development are significant factors influencing water supply services in Lusaka.
Unplanned land development has also led to challenges in water supply services, particularly in areas with shallow water tables that are vulnerable to groundwater pollution.
